verdicts.why: No finding is about an attacker-controlled length field driving a buffer allocation made before the payload is confirmed present. The two findings are F01 (unbounded recursion depth in readFieldValue/readTable/readArray) and F02 (integer overflow when multiplying a network-read long by 1000 for a Date). The closest is F02, since it also concerns a raw numeric value read from the wire, but it is about arithmetic wraparound producing a wrong Date value, not about sizing or pre-allocating a buffer from a declared length. F01 exhausts the stack through nesting depth, not through a declared size driving heap allocation. Neither mentions readLongstr/readShortstr-style length-prefixed reads or any new byte[]/allocation sized by untrusted input.

verdicts.quote: Case 'F' at line 181 calls readTable(), which at line 150 calls readFieldValue() again. Case 'A' at line 184 calls readArray(), which at line 245 calls readFieldValue() again. An attacker can craft a protocol message with deeply nested tables and arrays (e.g., table containing array containing table containing array...) to trigger unbounded recursion and exhaust stack memory, causing StackOverflowError.
verdicts.why: F01 describes exactly the mechanism: the decoding routines readFieldValue, readTable and readArray call one another in a cycle, no depth counter bounds the recursion, and nesting depth in the attacker-supplied AMQP message controls how deep the cycle goes, exhausting the stack. That is the mechanism D1 names, not an incidental mention.
